prompt: What does the whiteness of the whale symbolize?
chosen:
How does it relate to the color white in general? How does it relate to the white whale in particular?

Melville makes much of the color white in the novel—white bones, ivory, sperm, and so on. But the whale itself is white, and this whiteness is connected to Ahab’s quest for the white whale in complicated ways. On the one hand, the whale is white like Ahab’s ivory leg, and this connection suggests that the whale is the object of Ahab’s revenge. On the other hand, the whale’s whiteness is connected with a sense of the infinite and the infinite greatness of God, and this connection associates the whale with God. In this way, the whale is connected both with Ahab’s hate and with his love, and this connection gives Ahab’s pursuit a fatal quality—it is both morally wrong and morally justified, and Ahab has no way to distinguish between the two.

chosen:
What is its purpose in the book? What is its symbolic value? How does it illuminate the novel as a whole?

The chapter on the whiteness of the whale serves two distinct purposes. On one level, it sets the stage for subsequent chapters and serves as a link between the whale and Ahab. On another level, it serves as a symbolic overview of the novel as a whole. As the novel unfolds, this whale becomes more and more real, while Ahab’s quest to destroy it becomes more and more of a symbol for something else—namely Ahab’s own pursuit of an all-powerful god. By exploring the symbolic value of the whale’s whiteness, Melville reveals the symbolic nature of Ahab’s quest and the novel as a whole.

prompt: What makes Pride and Prejudice enduringly popular?
chosen:
On one level, it is a love story and we all adore a happy ending, especially when it comes to the smitten pair of Elizabeth and Darcy. But the novel is much more than a romance; it is a comedy of manners and Austen has so much fun satirising the foolishness and vanity of the socialites of her day. This makes it a great read for those of us with a wicked, cynical sense of humour. And there is so much more to this novel than merely being ‘entertaining’ – it is also a social and psychological analysis of its characters and their times, and a critique of the way in which an individual’s beliefs and ideas can be shaped and limited by the society in which they live.

In this respect, _Pride and Prejudice_ can be regarded as a ‘portrait of an

engaged mind’ and in this case the portraitist is remarkably adept at

giving us a clear idea of how her mind works.
